title: Slide 1 · Unsupervised Learning, Clustering, and PCA
question: Ava logged (1, 2) hours. Bo logged (2, 1) and Cy logged (5, 6). Without seeing a single score, which log is closer to Ava’s?
answer: Bo differs by one hour on each measurement. Cy differs by four on each. Either ordinary distance or squared distance puts Bo closer. Nothing in that comparison tells us who earned a higher score.

title: Slide 2 · Read a row before choosing a method
question: How many rows would a fifth student add if they reported both measurements?
answer: One row. The number of columns stays at two because the measurements are unchanged.

title: Slide 3 · Assign each log to its nearest center
question: What does a cluster number tell us about performance on an exam?
answer: It identifies the nearest current center under these two measurements. We would need exam outcomes to check any link to performance.

title: Slide 4 · Move the centers and measure the improvement
question: Why can a center have 1.5 reading hours even if nobody recorded that value?
answer: The center summarizes two records with 1 and 2 hours. The mean can lie between observed values.

title: Slide 5 · Check what a cluster depends on
question: If we allow a center at each of the four distinct records, what happens to the training cost?
answer: Every row can have zero distance to a center. The cost falls to zero, but four representatives give us no compression of four records.

title: Slide 6 · Center the records and measure how features vary together
question: Why subtract the column means first?
answer: We want co-variation around the typical week. Centering gives zero to a typical feature value and separates variation from the location of the whole cloud.

title: Slide 7 · Rotate a line and compare the variance it retains
question: Could the vector (−1,−1)/√2 serve equally well as the principal direction?
answer: Yes. It points along the same line. Each projected coordinate changes sign and its squared value stays the same.

title: Slide 8 · Recover an approximate record from one coordinate
question: A tutor wants to distinguish equal totals with different reading/practice balances. Is one principal coordinate enough here?
answer: No. Ava and Bo have identical diagonal coordinates. Keep the original two features or retain the second component as well.

title: Slide 9 · Let two groups share responsibility for an observation
question: At 4 hours both densities are equal. What responsibilities result if the priors change to 0.75 and 0.25?
answer: The common density cancels. The responsibilities are 0.75 and 0.25. Equal distance alone cannot determine responsibilities when priors differ.

title: Slide 11 · From this module to the next
question: A principal direction preserves nearly all input variance. Does that guarantee it contains the feature needed to predict a label?
answer: No. Imagine the label only records which activity took more time. Ava and Bo project to the same coordinate but their labels differ. A supervised model can use the labels to favor a different feature.

title: Office hours · Why does PCA belong in machine learning when nobody supplied a target?
question: Why does PCA belong in machine learning when nobody supplied a target?
answer: The mean and projection direction are estimated from observed records. New records can be mapped into the resulting coordinate system. The criterion being fitted is retained variance rather than a score-prediction loss.

title: Office hours · How can I tell clustering and PCA apart?
question: How can I tell clustering and PCA apart?
answer: K-means gives Ava a group and a representative weekly log. PCA gives her a coordinate along a direction shared by everyone. You can ask how much squared variation each method loses, but the two representations answer different questions.

title: Office hours · Will a k-means run always find the lowest possible cost?
question: Will a k-means run always find the lowest possible cost?
answer: Assignment and mean-update steps can settle at a locally stable solution. Try several starts and compare costs for the same number of clusters. If a cluster receives no rows, its mean is undefined; the lab keeps that center in place and marks it empty.

title: Office hours · Why might software give slightly larger covariance values?
question: Why might software give slightly larger covariance values?
answer: The worked example divides by n=4 to describe the four observed weeks. A sample covariance estimate often uses n−1=3 instead. It scales every entry and eigenvalue by 4/3 here, leaving the directions and retained fraction unchanged.

title: Exercise 1
question: A new weekly log is (2,3). With centers A=(1,2) and B=(5,6), find both squared distances and assign the row.
answer: A costs (2−1)²+(3−2)²=2. B costs (2−5)²+(3−6)²=18. Choose A.

title: Exercise 2
question: A cluster contains (1,2), (2,1), and (3,3). Update its center and calculate its new sum of squared distances.
answer: Both means equal 2. Distances squared to (2,2) are 1, 1, and 2, so the new within-cluster cost is 4.

title: Exercise 3
question: Centered records have covariance matrix with rows (3,−2) and (−2,3). Which diagonal direction retains more variance?
answer: C(1,1)=(1,1), but C(1,−1)=(5,−5). The unit direction (1,−1)/√2 therefore retains variance 5, compared with 1 along (1,1)/√2. One coordinate tends to rise as the other falls.

title: Exercise 4
question: A researcher fits PCA to all records, including a reserved test set, before evaluating a prediction model. How would you redesign this?
answer: Estimate column means and principal directions from the training split. Apply those same values to the held-out records. Including the test inputs in the fit otherwise lets their distribution influence the representation used in evaluation.

title: Exercise 5
question: Two mixture components give densities 0.2 and 0.1 for a record. Their prior weights are 0.25 and 0.75. Which group gets the larger responsibility?
answer: Weighted densities are 0.05 and 0.075. Dividing by 0.125 gives 0.4 and 0.6. The second component wins despite having a lower density at this value.

title: Exercise 6
question: Two students interpret the two k-means centers as proof of two natural learning styles. What evidence do the logs actually provide?
answer: The chosen two-center model groups four weekly logs by two measured activities. A student could change clusters next week. Vary the measurements, units, number of centers and sample before claiming a stable pattern. No learning-style label was measured.
